canonicalExplanation.summary: **Container queries** let a component respond to the size of its **container**, not the whole screen. First mark an ancestor as a query container with `container-type: inline-size` (optionally `container-name`). Then `@container (min-width: 32rem) { … }` applies inside it. The same card can then be stacked in a narrow sidebar and side-by-side in a wide main area — on the same page. Always write a safe **baseline** that works without the query.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A course card should show its image beside the text when there's room. Media queries can't help: on a wide screen, the card might sit in a narrow sidebar *and* a wide main column at the same time. The card needs to know its own space. The same card switches to a side-by-side layout only when its panel container is wide enough. In this lesson you'll build and explain a component with a size-based container query and safe baseline.

```predict
{"question": "You write `@container (min-width: 32rem)` but never set `container-type` on any ancestor. What happens?", "options": ["It measures the card itself", "The query never matches — there's no query container"], "answer": 1, "why": "A container query needs an ancestor declared as a container. Without one, the styles inside simply don't apply."}
```

examples.title: One card, two layouts
examples.situation: The same card switches to a side-by-side layout only when its panel container is wide enough.
walkthrough: **Declare:** `.panel { container-type: inline-size; container-name: panel; }` on both the sidebar and the main column wrappers.
**Baseline:** the card stacks image above text — works anywhere, even without container-query support.
**Query:** `@container panel (min-width: 32rem)` makes it side by side; the browser will render the main-column card side by side and the sidebar card stacked, on the same screen.
examples.result: One card component adapts to each panel's width, independent of the viewport.

examples.title: The query that never fired
examples.situation: A developer writes `@container (min-width: 30rem) { .card { … } }` and sets `container-type` on `.card` itself.
walkthrough: The card is the container, so the query can only style the card's descendants.
The card's own grid never changes.
Fix: put `container-type: inline-size` on the card's wrapper (the panel), not the card.
examples.result: The card responds once its parent panel is the query container.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Container queries measure the component's own final size without any configured ancestor.
misconceptions.correction: A container query measures an ancestor that has been declared a query container with container-type, and applies styles to that container's descendants. Without a declared container, the query doesn't apply.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The query that never fired", why didn't the card's layout change?

analogy.example: A container query is like **furniture that adjusts to the room it's in**, not to the size of the whole building. The room (container) must have its measurements posted for the furniture to read them.
usefulFor: remembering the ancestor must be declared
components adapt to their own space
limitations: Furniture can't measure itself either — it reads the room.
The baseline is furniture that works in any room.

remediation.explanation: If a container query doesn't apply: **1) Is an ancestor declared with container-type? 2) Are you styling a descendant, not the container? 3) Does the name match?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Run the checks on "The query that never fired".

recap.summary: To build and explain a component with a size-based container query, declare an ancestor with container-type: inline-size (and a name), write a safe baseline layout, then add @container rules that style descendants when that container is wide enough. Use them for reusable components instead of viewport media queries.
